statement: A closed box measures 12 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. An ant walks on the outside of the box from one corner to the corner farthest from it. How long is the shortest such walk?

choices.misconception: I measured the straight line through the inside of the box, but the ant must stay on the surface.
I unfolded two faces so that the 12 cm and 2 cm edges lay in one line, which is not the best unfolding.
I unfolded two faces so that the 12 cm and 3 cm edges lay in one line, which is not the best unfolding.
I made the ant walk along three edges of the box.

hints: Unfold the two faces the ant crosses into one flat rectangle.
A shortest path over two faces becomes a straight line once those faces are unfolded flat. There are three essentially different unfoldings; compare all of them and keep the smallest diagonal.
The unfoldings give rectangles 12 by 5, 14 by 3 and 15 by 2. Find each diagonal.

solutions.reliable: The ant crosses two adjacent faces. Unfolded, they form a rectangle, and the shortest path is its diagonal. Pairing the edges in three ways gives rectangles 12 by (3 + 2), (12 + 2) by 3 and (12 + 3) by 2, with diagonals √169 = 13, √205 and √229. The smallest is 13 cm. The straight line through the box, √157, is shorter but not allowed. The transferable idea: unfold the surface, then compare every unfolding, because the best one joins the two shorter edges.
solutions.elegant: Always put the two shortest edges side by side: the diagonal of a 12 by 5 rectangle is 13.

whyOnTest: Surface paths test unfolding a solid into the plane and checking every unfolding, with the through-the-box length as the classic trap.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
